description: We are looking for anyone who is interested in this topic and passionate about building this system with us.
summary: On the way to Mars, a message to a doctor on Earth can take up to twenty minutes, and contact can be lost for days. Astronauts therefore need to notice health problems themselves. We developed SpaceHealth, an offline web app that learns each astronaut's normal values before launch and compares their daily wearable, sleep and radiation data with them. For each area it shows a clear status (normal, watch, act, or no reliable data), explains the evidence behind it, and gives the next steps, including when to contact the crew medical officer. It never diagnoses. The rules and numbers come from NASA standards and published spaceflight and wearable research, and the radiation module replays real NASA DONKI solar-storm records. We chose the detection method by comparing eight published approaches, locked its settings, and tested it once on forty new simulated missions: it flagged the illness by the first symptom in 25 and within a few days in 39. We also checked it on real smartwatch data from people who became ill. SpaceHealth supports NASA's goal of Earth-independent medical care for long missions.
details:
What it does SpaceHealth is a self-monitoring tool for astronauts on long missions. It learns each crew member's normal values from 14 days of measurements before launch and then checks three areas every day: physiological signals (overnight resting heart rate, heart-rate variability, skin temperature and reported symptoms), sleep, and radiation. Each area receives one of four statuses: Nominal, Watch, Act, or No reliable data — missing data is never shown as normal. Every status comes with the evidence (a chart against the person's own normal range), an action card with next steps, when to recheck and when to contact the onboard crew medical officer, and a short evidence-based self-care box (for example a planned nap after short sleep, or hygiene steps to protect crewmates). It does not diagnose disease.

How it works

  • Personal baseline: the median and robust spread of each person's preflight values, fixed for the whole mission so that a slow decline cannot become the new normal.
  • Physiological change: an EWMA control chart on resting heart rate raises Watch when a sustained rise appears; red-flag symptoms (fever, shortness of breath, chest pain, fainting, vision change) raise Act.
  • Sleep: Watch after two short nights compared with the person's own normal; Act when seven-night sleep debt reaches 8.16 hours, the equivalent of one night without sleep (Van Dongen et al., 2003).
  • Radiation: an immediate Act on any solar-particle-event warning, daily and cumulative dose, and a projection against NASA's 600 mSv career limit (NASA-STD-3001).
  • In flight, wearable, dosimeter and space-weather data would arrive automatically and the astronaut would add a one-minute symptom check-in. The prototype loads a complete simulated 180-day mission computed in advance, so it runs fully offline; the dashboard shows any mission day and can replay the mission.

How we tested it We built a simulator in which we know exactly when problems start (an illness-like change, a solar storm, a week of short sleep, exercise spikes and missing data), with effect sizes taken from published studies. We compared eight published detection methods using rules fixed in advance, chose one, locked its settings and ran a final test once on forty new simulated missions: the illness was flagged by the first symptom in 25 of 40 and within a few days in 39 of 40; every replayed solar-storm warning triggered an immediate Act; exercise spikes never escalated to Act. We also replayed four real NASA DONKI storm sequences (2017, 2021, May and October 2024; all checks passed) and ran the locked detector on real smartwatch data from 21 people with COVID-19, where it flagged 13 within a week of symptom onset, about twice the chance level. These are simulation and sanity-check results, not clinical validation.

Benefits and intended impact SpaceHealth supports Earth-independent medical operations, a stated NASA need for missions beyond the Moon. It needs little crew time, works without an internet connection, and every alert can be explained and traced to a source. The same personal-baseline approach could help Antarctic stations, submarines and remote workers on Earth.

What makes it creative Instead of comparing astronauts with population averages, it compares each person with themselves. It turns flags into concrete next steps and self-care, replays real NASA solar-storm timing, and openly reports its own misses and limits, including a "blind test mission" view that shows a late flag and a missed case.

Factors we considered Scientific honesty (every number is labelled as evidence-based, direction-only, placeholder or assumption), safety (no diagnoses, urgent alerts are never hidden, missing data is never shown as normal), the communication delay and blackouts on a Mars mission, crew workload, accessibility (status is never shown by colour alone; readable contrast) and privacy. Limitations: health performance is measured mainly on simulated data; bone health is not yet covered; immune and cardiovascular changes are covered only as early-warning signals; operational radiation thresholds are placeholders because the real values are not public.

Tools and languages Python 3.11 (NumPy, SciPy, pandas, scikit-learn, pydantic) for simulation, detection and testing; TypeScript, React, Vite, Zod and Recharts for the dashboard; JSON Schema for the shared data format; pytest and Vitest for about 265 automated tests; GitHub Actions for continuous testing; Vercel for hosting. No special hardware.

Team: Narayan Adhikari, Abhishek Sunil Tiwari, Shweta Sunil Tiwari.
